questions.prompt: Your `payment_method` enum covers `["card", "cash", "bank_transfer"]`. Documents now mention regional wallets, crypto, and buy-now-pay-later services — all being forced into `"card"`. How should the schema evolve?

choices.text: Add `"other"` to the enum, with a companion free-text field capturing the actual payment method.
Add the ten most common new payment methods to the enum every quarter, retiring the least-used existing categories to keep the list manageable.
Make the field free text entirely, and classify it into categories downstream instead.
Reject any document that mentions a payment method outside the current enum.

questions.explanation: The extensible-category pattern: `"other"` plus a detail field capturing the actual method — novel categories are represented faithfully, and the enum stays machine-readable. B chases reality quarterly and always trails it, while also discarding categories still in use. C pushes classification downstream, unsolved. D rejects valid business documents.

Use `tool_choice: "auto"` along with a prompt instruction to always extract structured data.
Use `tool_choice: "any"` — a tool call is guaranteed, and the model picks whichever extraction tool matches the document.
Run three separate pipeline lanes with a rules-based classifier routing documents up front, maintaining its keyword rules as new document variants appear.

questions.explanation: Multiple extraction schemas, unknown document type, structured output required: `tool_choice: "any"` — a tool call is guaranteed, and the model selects the schema fitting the document. questions.prompt: Contracts occasionally arrive with a stated term whose end date precedes its start date (drafting or OCR errors). Downstream date math silently produces negative durations. What extraction design surfaces the problem?

choices.text: Swap the two dates when the end precedes the start, since that's clearly the intended order.
Extract both dates exactly as stated, and set a `conflict_detected` boolean when the ordering can't be true, so a human resolves which value is wrong.
Reject any contract whose extracted dates are out of order before it reaches downstream systems.
Extract only the start date, deriving the end date from the contract's stated term length instead.

questions.explanation: Impossible source data is neither passed through silently nor silently corrected: extract as stated and flag with `conflict_detected` for review. A "fixes" data it cannot verify — the error might be in either field. C stalls legitimate documents over a flag-able condition. D derives from data already suspect.

questions.prompt: `signatory_date` keeps failing extraction on a batch of scanned agreements. Sampling shows the signature page simply wasn't scanned — the date isn't in the input. The retry system has been resubmitting these documents for days. What is the correct assessment?

choices.text: These retries cannot succeed — the date was never captured in the scan; stop retrying and route the batch for rescanning.
Raise the retry count and vary the prompt wording until the model manages to find the missing dates.
These retries would succeed with a larger context window feeding in more of the surrounding scanned pages, giving the model more material to search.
The field should be dropped from the schema entirely, since this batch couldn't produce it.

questions.explanation: The date isn't in the input, so no retry can extract it — days of resubmission bought nothing. Detect information-absent failures, stop retrying, and route to rescanning or accept a documented null. B and C retry harder at reading a page that was never scanned. D deletes a real business field because one batch was scanned badly.

questions.prompt: You added few-shot examples covering three vendors' invoice layouts. Extraction then also improved markedly on a fourth vendor whose layout none of the examples showed. What explains this?

choices.text: The fourth vendor's layout must simply happen to resemble one of the three example layouts closely.
The longer prompt produced by adding examples happened to help on its own, since longer prompts generally score better on this kind of task regardless of their content.
A model update shipped at the same time as the examples; the examples themselves were irrelevant.
Few-shot examples teach the underlying judgment involved, which the model generalizes to novel layouts.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach transferable judgment — how to locate and map fields across layout variation — which generalizes to unseen structures; that's why they beat exhaustive per-layout rules. A is possible but explains nothing generalizable and contradicts "markedly improved." B treats prompt length as the mechanism, which it isn't. C is an unfalsifiable coincidence that doesn't fit the pattern described.

choices.text: Preprocess every filing to convert its narrative sections into tables before extraction.
Run three separate extractors, one tuned to each presentation style, normalize their outputs to a common shape, and merge the results afterward.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating extraction from tabular, narrative, and footnote presentations, so the model learns the pattern across all three.
Restrict extraction to the tables, and flag narrative and footnote sections for human review.

questions.explanation: Structural variety (tables, narrative, footnotes) is the few-shot case: demonstrate correct extraction from each presentation and the model handles the spread. A presumes a reliable narrative-to-table converter — the original problem restated. B triples the pipeline to route around a single model's limitation. D shrinks automation to the easy subset.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Two workloads: (1) re-extracting your ten-year document archive with an improved schema, results needed "sometime this quarter"; (2) extracting data from documents customers upload during a live onboarding flow. Assign the APIs.

choices.text: Use the synchronous API for both workloads, since operating a single API end to end is simpler than maintaining two separate integration paths.
Batch API for the archive; synchronous API for the onboarding flow a customer is waiting on.
Batch for the onboarding flow since volume is high; synchronous for the archive.
Batch API for both workloads, since the pricing discount is too large to pass up.

questions.explanation: The archive is the Batch API's ideal customer: enormous, latency-tolerant, half price. Onboarding has a customer waiting — synchronous. A forfeits major savings for no operational reason. C parks live customers behind a no-SLA queue. D is backwards on one of the two.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Your contract guarantees extraction results within 36 hours of document receipt. Batch processing takes up to 24 hours. Documents arrive continuously. Which accumulation window keeps the guarantee?

choices.text: Accumulate for 8 hours — worst case 8 + 24 = 32 hours, within the 36-hour guarantee.
Accumulate for 24 hours — a single daily batch is the operationally cleanest schedule.
Accumulate for 16 hours, since batches usually complete in far less than the stated 24-hour maximum processing window in practice.
Accumulate for 48 hours, adding an expedite lane for documents that are already old.

questions.explanation: The guarantee must hold in the worst case: 8-hour accumulation + 24-hour processing = 32 ≤ 36 with margin. B gives 48 worst case. C's 16 + 24 = 40 breaches the SLA, and "usually faster" isn't a guarantee. D starts beyond the SLA and patches with an expedite lane.

Submit the batch at half the usual temperature setting, to be safe with a sensitive dataset.
Split the batch into two runs of 5,000 forms each, correcting the prompt between the two runs based on whatever errors the first half turns up.
Refine and verify the prompt on a representative sample via the synchronous API first.

questions.explanation: With a fixed budget, first-pass success is everything: refine the prompt on a representative sample synchronously, verify, then submit the batch. A spends the budget discovering flaws at full scale. B tweaks an unrelated generation parameter instead of validating correctness. C still burns half the budget on the unvalidated version.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Your extraction step ends with "double-check your extraction against the document" — and reports itself accurate. Auditors keep finding wrong values the self-check approved. What is the structural lesson?

choices.text: Give the self-check a few-shot example of a caught error, alongside a rubric listing common error types to watch for.
Run the self-check twice in the same session, escalating to a human whenever the two passes happen to disagree with each other.
Run verification as an independent instance, comparing output to source without the extractor's own context.
Self-checks work fine as long as you also request a confidence score alongside them.

questions.explanation: A model verifying its own extraction retains the reasoning that produced the errors — self-checks approve their own mistakes. Verification must be an independent instance comparing output to source without the extractor's context. A hands the same biased checker a rubric and an example. B repeats the biased check twice. D scores it without changing what's doing the checking.

choices.text: Exclude handwritten forms from the accuracy metric entirely, since they drag down the average.
Aggregate metrics mask segment failures — validate accuracy by document type and field before it justifies any downstream decision.
Have the dashboard show median accuracy instead of the mean across all documents.
96% is an accurate overall number, so no change to the process is required here.

questions.explanation: 96% aggregate coexisting with 61% on handwritten forms is exactly how aggregate metrics mask segment failures: validate by document type and field before the number justifies anything, and remediate the failing segment. A hides the problem from the metric instead of fixing it. C changes the statistic, not the blindness. D accepts a segment that's wrong 4 times in 10.

questions.prompt: After automating high-confidence extractions, you need an ongoing mechanism to catch error patterns the confidence model doesn't know about yet. What is it?

choices.text: Run a quarterly re-validation of the model against the original benchmark set.
Alert whenever confidence scores drift statistically from their historical baseline.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for continuous human review.
Add a user-facing "report an error" button on the downstream systems that consume the data, relying on customers to surface anything the model got wrong.

questions.explanation: Novel error patterns in the automated stream are caught by stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions with ongoing human review — measuring true error rates where no one otherwise looks. A can't contain patterns that didn't exist at benchmark time. B watches the scores, not the truth. D makes customers the QA layer.

questions.prompt: The model emits per-field confidence scores, and you plan to auto-accept above a threshold. A colleague proposes 0.9 "because it's high." What is the defensible way to choose?

choices.text: Calibrate against a labeled validation set: measure accuracy at each score level and set the threshold where it actually meets the requirement.
Adopt 0.9 as proposed, but review the first month of auto-accepted extractions by hand.
Pick 0.95 instead, splitting the difference between the proposal and maximum caution.
Average the last quarter's confidence scores and use that average as the threshold.

questions.explanation: Thresholds come from calibration: measure actual accuracy at each confidence level against labeled data, and set the cutoff (per field type if performance differs) where accuracy meets requirements. B and C are round numbers with different amounts of caution — neither is a measurement. D averages scores into a threshold with no connection to accuracy. --- *End of Practice Exam 10.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Every contributor must follow the same repository-wide naming and error-handling conventions in every Claude Code session. The guidance changes with the repository and should be reviewed in pull requests. Where should it live?

choices.text: In each contributor's personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which loads regardless of repository.
In an on-demand skill named `/standards` that a contributor must remember to invoke first.
In the repository's project-level `CLAUDE.md`, committed alongside the code, reviewed in pull requests, and versioned like any other file in the tree.
In an inline prompt block that gets pasted into the start of each new session before work begins.

questions.explanation: Shared, durable, repository-wide guidance belongs in the committed project `CLAUDE.md`, where it is versioned and reviewed like code. Personal memory loads regardless of which project is open, an on-demand skill can be skipped, and a re-pasted prompt drifts and gets forgotten.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Security conventions apply to every file named `*Controller.ts`, which appears under many unrelated packages. The conventions should load only when Claude edits those files. Which mechanism fits?

choices.text: A `.claude/rules/` file scoped with a `paths` glob matching `*Controller.ts` everywhere.
A `CLAUDE.md` placed in whichever package happens to contain the first controller file the team wrote.
A root `CLAUDE.md` section that lists the convention once and asks Claude to infer when it applies from surrounding context.
A slash command developers invoke before changing controllers, since no hook currently watches that path automatically.

questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule with a glob follows matching files across unrelated directories and loads only for them. A single-package memory file misses scattered locations, a root-level note relies on inference instead of automatic scoping, and a manual command is easy to forget even without a competing hook.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: A team-wide dependency audit is run only before quarterly releases. It produces lengthy exploratory output that should not remain in the implementation conversation. How should it be packaged?

choices.text: As a large block appended to the root `CLAUDE.md` so every session always carries the audit checklist.
As a user-level command each contributor must separately install and keep synchronized across their own `~/.claude` configuration.
As a path rule that reloads its exploratory instructions whenever any dependency manifest file happens to be read.
As a project skill configured with `context: fork`, invoked only before releases.

questions.explanation: An occasional, verbose workflow fits a skill, and `context: fork` isolates its exploration so it never bloats the main conversation. Always-loaded memory wastes context every session, a per-contributor command fragments and drifts, and a rule tied to manifest reads fires far more often than the intended quarterly cadence.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

questions.prompt: A deployment tool may run only when its arguments contain both an approved change-ticket ID and the current maintenance-window identifier. Prompt reminders have already been bypassed. What should enforce the rule?

choices.text: A stronger warning added to `CLAUDE.md` asking Claude to double-check both IDs.
A `PreToolUse` hook that inspects the tool's arguments before execution and blocks the call outright unless both the ticket ID and the window ID are present.
A path-scoped rule that loads reminder text whenever a deployment manifest file is opened.
A custom command that prints the policy and asks the operator to confirm both values before deployment begins.

questions.explanation: Enforcement that depends on live tool arguments must be deterministic and run before the tool executes, which is what a `PreToolUse` hook provides. Warnings and printed policy text remain advisory, and a path-scoped rule cannot inspect the arguments a running tool receives.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

`~/.claude/commands/rewrite-commit.md` in your personal user configuration, kept invisible to the rest of the team and never checked into the shared repository.
A personal heading inside the shared project `CLAUDE.md` that only you are supposed to read.
A prompt definition added to `.mcp.json` alongside the team's server configuration.

questions.explanation: User-scoped commands are personal and are not distributed through the repository. A project command would affect teammates, while `CLAUDE.md` and MCP configuration are different mechanisms entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Turn the document into a dedicated MCP server just so this one file can be fetched on demand.
Load it through a path rule that fires whenever any source file, not just this one, gets edited.
Reference it with `@docs/legacy-auth-flow.md` directly in the current prompt for this task only.

questions.explanation: An `@` reference supplies a known relevant file to the current task without permanently consuming future context. The other choices make one-time context durable or introduce unrelated infrastructure that fires on unrelated edits.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

A personal skill kept in `~/.claude/skills/`, invoked manually by whoever remembers it.
A root-level slash command developers must remember to run first.
An MCP resource that stores the conventions as data a server happens to expose.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

questions.prompt: After every file edit, the team must run the formatter and immediately return any formatting failure to Claude, regardless of whether Claude remembered to run it. Which mechanism provides that behavior?

choices.text: A formatting paragraph added to `CLAUDE.md`, trusting Claude to remember to invoke it after every edit.
A `PreToolUse` hook attached to Read operations, checked before the file is even opened.
A `PostToolUse` hook matched to file-edit events, run automatically after every edit completes.
An `@` reference pointing at the formatter's configuration file for context only.

questions.explanation: `PostToolUse` runs after the edit and can invoke the formatter and return failures to Claude every time. A prose instruction is probabilistic, attaching the hook to Read fires at the wrong event, and an `@` reference does not execute checks.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Claude's CSV converter mishandles quoted commas. Repeating “support all valid CSV” has not helped. Which feedback is most likely to produce a reliable correction?

choices.text: Ask for more reasoning effort on the retry, without ever showing Claude the failing example.
Ask for a completely different implementation with no constraints, then eyeball it against a few CSV files that already worked.
Add the recurring issue permanently to user-level memory so future sessions inherit the note.
Provide the failing input, the current output, the exact expected output, and the relevant regression test.

questions.explanation: A concrete failing input, observed output, expected output, and regression test give Claude an exact correction target and preserve the fix. Asking for more effort without evidence, a from-scratch rewrite compared only by eye, and permanent memory notes do not pin down the transformation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: You are designing an unfamiliar cache invalidation layer and have not decided how freshness, failure recovery, or multi-region writes should behave. Which refinement technique should come before implementation?

Generate the simplest cache implementation, let production incidents reveal the real requirements, and record whatever behavior results as policy.
Put a one-line "use best practices" note in `CLAUDE.md` and move straight to direct execution.
Ask several agents to each implement a different alternative before the acceptance criteria have been clarified.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern surfaces missing product and failure-mode decisions before code hardens accidental assumptions. Implementing first and letting incidents define policy, or multiplying implementations before criteria exist, cannot resolve requirements that have not been decided.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Send all three together in one message, since batching every kind of feedback is always the more efficient approach.
Describe the two interacting API changes together with their shared constraint, and raise the unrelated spelling fix separately.
Add all three issues as notes in `CLAUDE.md` and let whichever session picks it up next decide the order.

questions.explanation: Interacting issues should be presented together with their shared constraints, while an independent issue can be handled separately. Universal "always batch" or "always sequence" rules ignore dependency structure.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.

Write, which creates or overwrites a file rather than searching anything.
Edit, which modifies an existing file's contents rather than searching for one.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: An unfamiliar service has thousands of files. You need to understand how requests reach `authorizePayment` without flooding the context window. What is the strongest exploration strategy?

choices.text: Search for the symbol and likely entry points, Read only the matching files, then follow relevant imports incrementally.
Read every file under the service in full before forming any hypothesis about the call path.
Glob only for filenames containing "payment," infer the flow from names, and treat import order as a proxy for runtime behavior.
Run the entire test suite repeatedly and try to infer the architecture from pass/fail output alone.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.

choices.text: Start a completely blank session and reconstruct the repository map from scratch.
Fork the session even though no divergent approach or comparison is actually needed here.
Copy only yesterday's final assistant response into a brand-new conversation.
Resume the named session directly with `--resume <session-name>`, since the repository map is still accurate.

questions.explanation: Named resumption is appropriate when prior context and tool results remain valid and the goal is unchanged. Forking is for divergence, and starting over or copying a single response discards reliable work.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.

choices.text: Resume unchanged, since the conversation still contains the old tool results and the transcript can identify which files still matter.
Fork the stale session and treat both resulting branches as equally reliable going forward.
Start fresh with a written summary of durable conclusions, identify changed areas, and re-read the affected files.
Discard both the durable architectural conclusions and all prior repository context.

questions.explanation: Major file changes make old tool results stale, so a fresh session seeded with durable conclusions and targeted re-reading is safer than resuming or forking stale evidence. Discarding the durable architectural conclusions along with the stale evidence is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

choices.text: Put the server and the literal shared token directly in root `CLAUDE.md`, then ask each engineer to copy the token to a local file first.
Commit the server definition in project `.mcp.json` and reference an environment variable for the token.
Ask every engineer to create an unrelated personal skill that has nothing to do with the issue tracker.
Store the server definition only in one maintainer's personal `~/.claude.json`.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: One developer is evaluating an unstable local MCP server that nobody else should see yet. Where should the definition live?

choices.text: In project `.mcp.json`, marked with a comment that calls it experimental.
In the root `CLAUDE.md`, on the theory that teammates will simply ignore it.
In `.claude/rules/` with a path scoped to that developer's files.
In that developer's personal, user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, which is never committed or seen by anyone else on the team.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Claude Code connects to three configured MCP servers. A teammate proposes writing a router that activates exactly one server for each request. What should you explain?

choices.text: Tools from every connected server are discovered together; selection follows their contracts and context, not a single active server.
Project-scoped servers automatically disable any user-scoped server whenever both happen to be configured for the same session at once.
Claude Code can only discover the first server listed in `.mcp.json` and needs a manual reconnect for any other tool.
MCP resources, rather than tool contracts, are what determine which server becomes active for a request.

questions.explanation: Tools from every connected MCP server are discovered together and made available to the agent; clear contracts and context guide selection. There is no required one-active-server toggle, and MCP resources do not gate which server runs.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A committed `.mcp.json` currently contains a plaintext production token. What is the correct credential pattern?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token and leave the encoded value in the same committed file.
Move the token into a code comment on the theory that Claude will not read comments.
Replace it with environment-variable expansion, such as `${INTERNAL_MCP_TOKEN}`, so the secret never gets committed to version control.
Put the token inside a project slash command definition instead.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret outside version control while leaving the server definition shareable. Encoding, comments, and slash commands do not secure a committed credential.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

Whenever more than one developer will share an integration, so its definition stays identical across every machine and repository.
Whenever the integration happens to authenticate using an environment variable.
Always, since community servers can never be scoped to a single project.

questions.explanation: Existing maintained servers are preferred for standard integrations; custom work is warranted for team-specific contracts or behavior not otherwise available. Sharing across developers or using an environment variable does not by itself require a custom server.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that fires after each discovery call completes.
A forced write tool that records catalog lookups somewhere else.
MCP resources describing the available services and their schemas.
A larger user-level `CLAUDE.md` containing a copy of the live catalog data.

questions.explanation: MCP resources expose catalogs and schema structures without repeated exploratory tool calls. A hook only reacts after a call already happened, and copying live catalogs into memory creates stale, bloated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

Grep for the literal text `FROM`, since that line appears in most Dockerfiles.
Edit the build configuration to see which file responds.
Glob using filename patterns that match all three naming variants at once, across every directory in the repository.

questions.explanation: Glob is designed for matching file paths and naming variants. Grep searches contents, reading every root is slower, and Edit is for changing files, not discovering them.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Glob found four candidate configuration files. You now need the complete surrounding structure of one 120-line file before deciding where a setting is inherited. What should you use?

Read the selected file in full to see how the setting sits within its surrounding structure.
Write a brand-new replacement configuration before understanding the original.
Bash-delete the other three candidate files to simplify the decision.

questions.explanation: Once candidates are narrowed, Read supplies the selected file's full local context. A single Grep match can hide inheritance structure, and writing or deleting files is premature before the original is understood.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A production log contains the exact message `permission cache exhausted`, and you need to locate where that text is emitted. Which tool is most direct?

choices.text: Glob for files whose names merely contain the word "cache."
Read through the entire repository sequentially until the string turns up.
Grep for the exact message text across the codebase.
Edit likely logging files one at a time until the message changes.

questions.explanation: An exact log string is a content-search problem, so Grep is direct. A filename guess and an exhaustive sequential read are both weaker, and Edit should follow diagnosis, not replace it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: You must trace how a CLI command reaches a database adapter in an unfamiliar repository. Which sequence best manages context?

choices.text: Read every Python file first, then search only once context is nearly full, and infer the route from whichever file was read last.
Locate command registration with Grep or Glob, Read the matches, and follow only the relevant imports and calls.
Infer the route from directory names alone and skip reading file contents entirely.
Ask a generic coding question about database adapters without citing any repository evidence.

questions.explanation: Incremental discovery narrows candidates before reading and follows only evidence-bearing relationships. Reading everything exhausts context, while inferring the route from names or asking without repository evidence is unreliable.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Claude confuses `search_source_code` with `search_runbooks`. Both descriptions currently say “search company content.” What is the best first correction?

choices.text: Force `search_source_code` to run for every query that merely contains the word "error."
Put both operations behind one third, even more generic tool simply named `search`.
Give the agent several more overlapping tools and let it call all of them before deciding, after the fact, which result actually answered the question.
Rewrite each description with distinct use cases, inputs, outputs, examples, boundaries, and when to prefer the other tool.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the model's primary selection signal and should differentiate purpose, formats, outputs, examples, edges, and neighboring tools. Forced keyword routing, generic consolidation, and giving the agent even more overlapping tools all preserve the ambiguity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: `analyze_content` handles web snippets while `analyze_document` handles uploaded files, but their names and descriptions overlap. What redesign most directly improves selection?

choices.text: Rename the first tool to a web-specific operation and make both contracts explicitly source-specific.
Keep the overlap, add "choose carefully" to the system prompt, and have Claude explain its choice only after the tool already ran.
Randomize which of the two tools runs and compare the outputs afterward.
Force both tools to run on every single item regardless of its source.

questions.explanation: Source-specific names and contracts move the distinction into the interface the model selects from. A system-prompt warning that is checked only after the tool already ran, randomness, and always calling both tools do not remove the overlapping semantics.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Detailed tool descriptions look correct, yet a system prompt says “for any investigation, always begin with the archive tool.” Claude keeps ignoring a better live-search tool. What should you inspect?

choices.text: Whether the archive tool's JSON schema lists its properties alphabetically and which server happened to connect first.
Keyword-sensitive prompt instructions that override or bias the model's normal tool selection.
Whether the two tools happen to live on different MCP servers entirely.
Whether the response token limit is set high enough for the archive tool's output.

questions.explanation: System-prompt wording can create keyword associations that override good descriptions. Schema property ordering, which server a tool lives on, and response length do not explain the mandated archive preference.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A source-control MCP tool times out. The agent must know whether to retry and what operation failed. What should the tool return?

choices.text: A successful empty list, so the workflow just continues as if nothing happened.
The text "something went wrong" with no error flag or validation marker, plus a `CLAUDE.md` note asking Claude to guess whether the string is data or failure.
`isError` plus a transient category, retryability, the attempted operation, a safe description, and a suggested next action.
Only the provider's raw, unfiltered stack trace.

questions.explanation: A structured error type, retryability, the attempted action, and next steps let the agent choose a recovery path. Empty success hides failure, text with no error flag or validation marker is not actionable, and a raw trace is unsafe and incomplete.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A code search completes successfully and finds no references. How should the tool represent this outcome?

choices.text: As a retryable transient error, purely because the result set happens to be empty.
As a permission error, so the coordinator spends time investigating access.
As a business-rule failure that requires human escalation before anything continues.
As a successful empty result, clearly distinct from any tool failure, error, or timeout that the coordinator would otherwise need to retry.

questions.explanation: No matches is a valid successful query result and must remain distinct from access or operational failures. Mislabeling it prompts wasteful retries or unnecessary escalation.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A compliance review always checks the same four known controls, while an incident investigation must branch based on each new log or dependency discovered. Which design is appropriate?

choices.text: Dynamic decomposition for both, since every agent workflow should branch on new evidence.
One large prompt for both, in order to avoid any coordination overhead between steps.
A fixed chain for both, so the step count stays predictable and auditability outranks evidence discovered mid-investigation.
A fixed chain for the repeatable control review, and dynamic decomposition for the investigation.

questions.explanation: Known repeatable stages suit a fixed chain, while evidence-driven incident work needs adaptive decomposition. One decomposition style is not optimal for both predictable and open-ended work, and a single unstructured prompt loses the benefit of either approach.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: The request is “add comprehensive tests to this unknown legacy service.” What should the coordinator do first?

choices.text: Generate one test file for every source file immediately, before looking at any of them.
Map the service, identify high-impact behavior and dependencies, then create subtasks that adapt to what the map reveals.
Apply the same fixed list of unit-test prompts used on every repository, and rerun it unchanged even after a test exposes a new dependency.
Delegate the whole task to a single test-writer and prohibit any further exploration.

questions.explanation: An unknown legacy system must first be mapped so high-impact behavior and dependencies can drive the testing plan. Immediate file-by-file generation, or a fixed prompt list that never updates even after new dependencies surface, is a guess that can miss integration risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A simple factual query needs one authoritative source, but the coordinator always invokes search, document analysis, statistics, synthesis, and report agents. What is the best change?

choices.text: Keep the full pipeline running but shorten every agent's response so latency and cost stay predictable regardless of the query.
Cache every specialist's most recent answer for reuse on the next request.
Let the coordinator select only the specialists justified by the query and intermediate findings.
Replace every specialist with one unrestricted general-purpose agent.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should scale delegation to query complexity and what is discovered along the way. Shortening every agent's output or caching stale answers does not remove an unnecessary full pipeline.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A broad market study omits regional regulation because the coordinator decomposed it only by product feature. How should decomposition be improved?

choices.text: Partition the full scope across complementary dimensions or source types, then verify coverage before synthesis.
Ask the synthesis agent to invent a regulatory section from general knowledge and label it an informed estimate.
Make every existing subtask longer in length without changing what it actually covers.
Remove the coverage requirement entirely so it matches whatever research was actually gathered.

questions.explanation: Broad work needs complementary scope partitioning and a coverage check so no major dimension vanishes. Longer subtasks cannot recover an unassigned region, and synthesis must not fabricate one from general knowledge.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: An open-ended performance investigation has not yet established which component is slow. What is the strongest initial subtask?

choices.text: Rewrite the database layer immediately, since it is commonly the slow component, even before any measurement confirms it.
Ask every specialist to optimize whichever component it happens to favor.
Measure and map the request path first, then generate prioritized subtasks from the observed bottlenecks.
Execute a fixed sequence of generic optimizations regardless of where the actual bottleneck lies.

questions.explanation: Measurement and mapping identify actual bottlenecks, after which subtasks can adapt to evidence. Rewriting a commonly-slow component pre-emptively, or running generic optimizations, starts from unsupported assumptions.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Forty files need the same predictable local checklist, followed by one cross-file compatibility review. Which decomposition best preserves depth?

choices.text: Run focused per-file passes and then a separate integration pass across all forty files.
Use an open-ended dynamic investigation for every single file even though every stage is already known in advance.
Put all forty files into one prompt and ask Claude to divide its attention evenly across them.
Skip the integration pass entirely, since every individual file already passed its local checklist.

questions.explanation: Predictable local checks benefit from focused per-file passes, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file behavior. One shared mega-prompt dilutes attention, and treating open-ended investigation as necessary for known stages, or skipping integration, both waste the structure that already exists.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A dependency audit discovers midway that two services share a generated client, invalidating several planned subtasks. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Finish the original task list before acknowledging the dependency, so the plan stays comparable with prior audit runs.
Revise the plan and generate replacement subtasks that account for the shared client.
Restart the entire investigation from zero without preserving any valid findings already produced.
Hide the discovery from the specialists so their assignments remain stable.

questions.explanation: Adaptive plans change when a newly discovered dependency invalidates prior assumptions, preserving still-valid findings while replacing affected work. Finishing the stale plan for comparability, restarting from zero, and hiding the discovery are all wasteful or dishonest.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Which coordinator behavior most clearly distinguishes adaptive decomposition from a fixed workflow?

choices.text: It uses the same specialists in a different order each run while keeping the predefined task list and completion conditions fixed.
It runs every predefined step in parallel instead of one after another.
It asks specialists for longer reports whenever the evidence gathered so far is thin.
It creates or revises subtasks in response to intermediate discoveries and remaining coverage gaps.

questions.explanation: Creating and revising subtasks from intermediate findings is the defining adaptive behavior. Reordering, parallelizing, or lengthening a still-fixed task list does not change what work actually gets generated.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Initial synthesis is strong but lacks evidence for one geography. What should an iterative coordinator do?

choices.text: Identify the gap, delegate a targeted follow-up search, then resynthesize with the new evidence.
Add a generic disclaimer to the report and stop despite the gap being recoverable.
Restart every completed subtask from scratch rather than only the affected section.
Ask the synthesis agent to fill the section without sources, citing material that never covered that geography.

questions.explanation: Iterative orchestration evaluates synthesis, identifies a specific gap, commissions targeted evidence, and resynthesizes. Disclaiming the gap, restarting unaffected subtasks, or inventing uncited content all skip a recoverable refinement step.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A specialist repeatedly maps “active users” to total registered accounts. Which feedback is most useful?

choices.text: Tell the specialist to simply think harder about what a metric means.
Raise the specialist's maximum output length so its reports run longer.
Replace the agent without describing the observed failure, and ask the replacement to guess the intended definition from old reports.
Provide representative inputs, the incorrect mappings, the desired mappings, and a precise definition of "active."

questions.explanation: Examples of the failure and desired mapping plus an exact definition teach the disputed boundary. Generic effort, a longer output limit, or a silent agent swap supplies no corrective evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Three findings arise from the same mistaken date-window assumption and will interact if fixed separately. How should the coordinator request refinement?

choices.text: Send each issue in isolation and withhold the shared assumption so each specialist optimizes its own correction independently.
Batch the related issues in one detailed request that explains their common dependency.
Fix only the single easiest finding and leave the rest of the interacting issues untouched.
Add the errors to permanent user memory instead of addressing them in this session.

questions.explanation: Related failures caused by one shared assumption should be evaluated together so the fix is coherent. Isolating them hides the interaction, fixing only one leaves the rest broken, and permanent memory is not an issue tracker.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You resume a research session after editing three previously analyzed parsers. Most other context remains valid. What should you tell the agent?

choices.text: Say nothing, since resumption is assumed to automatically detect every filesystem change on its own.
Re-read the entire repository from scratch, since targeted recovery is assumed to be impossible.
Name the three changed parsers, request targeted re-analysis of just those files, and explicitly retain the unaffected earlier findings.
Trust the old parser outputs, since named resumption is assumed to snapshot the filesystem before the next answer.

questions.explanation: A resumed agent must be told what changed so it can refresh affected evidence without repeating valid exploration. Session history does not automatically know about filesystem changes, and assuming otherwise in either direction wastes work or trusts stale output.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You want two independent research strategies to begin from the same accepted source map without contaminating one another. What mechanism fits?

choices.text: Resume the same session concurrently in two separate terminals.
Copy only the original user prompt into two brand-new blank sessions.
Run both research strategies sequentially within one single conversation.
Use `fork_session` to branch both strategies independently from the same shared, accepted baseline.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` preserves the accepted baseline while isolating divergent reasoning. Concurrent resume in two terminals shares the same branch, a blank session loses the baseline, and sequential work in one conversation contaminates the comparison.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A research agent has `search_news` and `search_academic`, but the latter is almost never chosen even for peer-reviewed-evidence requests. What should its description add?

choices.text: A promise that it always outperforms every other available tool, plus a blanket instruction to prefer it whenever the user requests credible or peer-reviewed evidence.
Its indexed sources, accepted query and date inputs, output metadata, example academic requests, and explicit contrast with news search.
Internal implementation details that have nothing to do with when to select it.
A requirement that both search tools run together on every single query.

questions.explanation: Selection improves when the academic tool says what it indexes, how to query it, what it returns, and when it wins over news search. Boasts and a blanket preference instruction, irrelevant implementation trivia, and mandatory dual calls are not useful boundaries.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A search specialist sees a transient timeout that succeeds on a safe local retry. What error-handling structure best protects coordinator context?

choices.text: Let the specialist recover locally; propagate only unresolved failure context, attempts, and partial results.
Propagate every first failure immediately, let the coordinator retry it, and preserve a full transcript of every attempt in the main context.
Hide all failures from the coordinator, including permanent ones that will never resolve on their own.
Terminate every subagent the moment any single tool call reports an error, without any recovery hook of its own.

questions.explanation: Specialists should recover locally from safe transient failures and spare coordinator context; unresolved errors should include attempts and usable partial results. Immediate propagation of every first failure, and total suppression of even permanent errors, are both brittle.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Invoice extraction works on the layout used in the prompt but fails when totals appear in tables, footnotes, or sidebars. What is the strongest improvement?

choices.text: Make every field required so Claude searches harder for it.
Retry the identical prompt repeatedly until one run happens to succeed.
Add several worked examples across different layouts, with normalization guidance, while keeping the schema-based tool output.
Replace tool use with free-form prose and require downstream code to parse whichever layout-specific explanation the model returns.

questions.explanation: Diverse positive examples teach field-location patterns across layouts, while normalization guidance and schema-based output preserve consistency. Repeating an identical prompt and making every field required do not teach layout variation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Dates appear as `03/04/26`, `4 March 2026`, and `2026-03-04`, while downstream systems require ISO 8601. What should accompany the schema?

choices.text: Explicit normalization instructions, including how to represent genuinely ambiguous dates rather than silently guessing.
Copy every date string unchanged, then have downstream systems infer the locale from the customer's account and the vendor's country instead of normalizing anything centrally.
A higher confidence threshold applied to date fields, with no explicit format rule at all.
A retry policy that simply omits the original date on the next attempt.

questions.explanation: The prompt must state the canonical format and define what to do when source notation is ambiguous. Leaving locale inference to downstream systems, a confidence threshold with no format rule, and a retry that drops the original date all fail to normalize centrally.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Some contracts legitimately contain no renewal date. The current required string field causes invented dates. What is the best correction?

choices.text: Keep the field required, add "do not hallucinate" to the prompt, and rely on downstream validation to reject any fabricated date every single run.
Make the field optional or nullable and instruct the model to use null when the source is silent.
Reject every contract that lacks a renewal date outright.
Derive a placeholder date from the contract's signing date instead.

questions.explanation: Optional or nullable fields faithfully represent genuine absence and remove pressure to fabricate. Rejection or deriving a placeholder date invents a business rule the source does not support.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Résumé extraction works for conventional corporate résumés but misses existing education and publication fields on academic CVs. Which change is most likely to generalize?

choices.text: Add a rule for the exact CV that failed and a new exception for every additional university template.
Force every missing field to an empty string rather than leaving it absent.
Run the same prompt more times and manually pick whichever output looks the most complete.
Add representative examples showing the same target fields across corporate, academic, and international layouts.

questions.explanation: Representative layout diversity teaches transferable extraction behavior across document families. A one-off rule overfits, forced empty strings hide the gap rather than close it, and re-running the same prompt and picking by eye does not fix the underlying pattern.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A scanned form omitted the page containing the requested identifier. Validation fails on every retry. What should the system do?

choices.text: Recognize that the information is absent, stop retrying, and route the document to rescanning, null handling, or human review.
Retry indefinitely using progressively stronger wording in the prompt.
Ask Claude to infer the identifier from neighboring records and label it model-generated so downstream teams know it was not scanned.
Mark the extraction successful and fill the field with a fabricated placeholder value.

questions.explanation: Retries cannot recover content missing from the source, so the system must stop and choose an operational path such as rescanning, null, or review. Guessing from neighboring records and indefinite retries both manufacture confidence without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: An extraction is schema-valid but fails a business check because line-item totals do not equal the stated subtotal. What should a corrective follow-up include?

choices.text: Only the phrase "try again," with no other context attached.
Provide only the failed subtotal and a generic instruction to change whichever value looks least plausible.
The original document, failed extraction, and specific validation discrepancy.
A random alternative subtotal chosen because it happens to pass validation.

questions.explanation: Corrective retries need the evidence, failed candidate, and exact validation error so the model can repair the semantic defect. A vague instruction or a value chosen only because it happens to validate cannot ground the correction.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Tool use guarantees that output conforms to the JSON schema, but customer names are occasionally placed in the vendor field. What does this demonstrate?

choices.text: Strict schemas eliminate both syntax errors and semantic extraction mistakes.
Semantic validation and representative examples are still needed after structural compliance.
The schema should be removed entirely, since it apparently caused the field swap.
A larger output token limit will correct the field's meaning.

questions.explanation: A schema guarantees shape, not that evidence was mapped to the correct field. Semantic validation and representative examples still define meaning and catch swaps; removing the schema or raising the token limit addresses neither problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Payment methods are represented by a fixed enum, but valid new methods appear regularly. How should the schema avoid forced misclassification?

choices.text: Include an `other` value with a detail field, and an `unclear` representation when the source is genuinely ambiguous.
Map every unfamiliar method to the closest existing category and update a hard-coded list every quarter, folding new methods into old normalization rules.
Reject every document containing a payment method the schema does not already list.
Replace the entire schema-based response format with free-form prose instead.

questions.explanation: `other` plus detail preserves novel valid values, while `unclear` represents ambiguity without guessing. Nearest-category mapping into a hand-maintained list, outright rejection, and dropping the schema for prose all lose source truth.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A document has clear header fields but an illegible handwritten approval box. Routing is currently based on one document-level confidence average. What is better?

choices.text: Randomly review ten percent of documents regardless of actual field quality.
Review every document and require the reviewer to re-enter every header field as well as interpret the approval box.
Accept every document whose average confidence score exceeds 0.9.
Route based on field-level confidence, field risk, and the handwritten ambiguity while allowing clear fields to proceed.

questions.explanation: Field-level routing isolates the ambiguous, risky approval box while preserving clear header extraction. A document average can hide critical field uncertainty, and blanket or random review wastes effort re-checking fields that were already clear.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: The team proposes auto-accepting fields above confidence 0.92 because the number “sounds safe.” How should the threshold be selected?

choices.text: Use 0.99 for every field without ever testing it against real outcomes.
Average whatever confidence values the model produced last week.
Calibrate scores against labeled outcomes by field and segment, then set thresholds that meet the accuracy target.
Let each individual model response choose and report its own threshold without any calibration, and have downstream systems store and trust that self-reported number.

questions.explanation: Confidence scores become actionable only after calibration against labeled outcomes at the relevant field and segment. An intuitive fixed number, a rolling average, and a self-reported per-response threshold all have no demonstrated relationship to accuracy.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: High-confidence extractions now bypass normal human review. How can the team detect new error patterns that the confidence model does not recognize?

choices.text: Review only the outputs that already came back with low confidence.
Continuously review a stratified random sample of auto-accepted outputs.
Trust the original benchmark indefinitely without ever re-checking it.
Retry a random sample without human labels and treat agreement between the two runs as proof the original was correct.

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling of auto-accepted output detects blind spots and distribution drift that confidence alone misses. Reviewing only known low-confidence failures, trusting an old benchmark, or comparing unlabeled reruns cannot reveal unknown high-confidence errors.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Which review policy best uses document characteristics and ambiguity?

choices.text: Route every hundredth document to whichever reviewer is next in a random queue.
Review every field in low-confidence documents with one generalist, even when only a single field is actually ambiguous.
Assign reviewers strictly by arrival order to keep the routing logic simple.
Route uncertain or high-risk fields to reviewers with relevant expertise, using confidence and source characteristics as signals.

questions.explanation: Effective routing combines ambiguity, field risk, source characteristics, and reviewer expertise. Random, arrival-order, or aggregate-only routing ignores where the uncertainty actually resides.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: The model confuses `extract_invoice` and `extract_purchase_order` when both documents contain totals and vendor names. What is the best tool-interface improvement?

choices.text: Give each tool explicit document cues, unique outputs, boundary examples, and guidance for distinguishing the two formats.
Force invoice extraction to run for every financial document regardless of its actual type.
Rename both tools to shorter, more generic names than they already have.

Ask downstream code to infer the document type after the fact from whichever fields happen to be populated most often during extraction and apply ad hoc normalization there, rather than fixing the tool contracts themselves.

questions.explanation: Similar document tools need explicit discriminators, examples, and distinct output contracts. Forcing one tool as the default, shortening both names, and having downstream code guess the type after the fact all leave the selection ambiguity intact.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A refund extraction requests an amount prohibited by policy. Retrying cannot change the policy result. What should the tool surface?

choices.text: A transient retryable error with unlimited attempts, skipping validation of whether the failure is actually temporary, and treating temporary glitches and permanent policy outcomes as one recovery path.
A successful empty response with no indication that anything was declined.
A non-retryable business error with a customer-safe explanation, a reason code, and the permitted next action.
Only an internal policy stack trace exposed straight to the caller.

questions.explanation: A policy violation is a non-retryable business outcome and should include a safe explanation, a reason code, and an allowed alternative. Treating it as transient wastes calls, empty success conceals the reason, and a raw stack trace is unsafe.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: An extraction tool cannot open a restricted document collection. Which response gives the agent the clearest recovery path?

choices.text: A generic "operation failed" message with no further detail.
A permission error, typed as non-retryable until access changes, with a suggestion to request access or escalate.
A valid, empty extraction object returned as if the call succeeded.
A transient category that keeps retrying, coordinated through a retry hook, until the same restricted collection has failed a fixed number of times before escalation.

questions.explanation: A permission error typed as non-retryable tells the agent that retries will not help until access changes and gives a concrete escalation path. A generic message, a silent empty success, and a retry loop dressed up with a "retry hook" all drive the wrong behavior. *End of Practice Exam 13.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A customer says, “My replacement never arrived, and now the original card was charged again.” Identity is already verified, and the shipment and charge investigations are independent until the final response. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Classify the case by whichever concern the customer mentions first, run that fixed workflow to completion, and defer the other concern until it closes.
Create separate shipment and billing subtasks, run them concurrently, then synthesize one coordinated case resolution for the customer.
Escalate the entire case immediately, since any request naming more than one concern is treated as exceeding autonomous scope.
Let the shipping and billing specialists each reply to the customer directly, without coordinator synthesis.

questions.explanation: Independent concerns can be investigated in parallel once identity is confirmed, and coordinator synthesis produces one coherent resolution. Serializing by first-mentioned concern, blanket escalation, and unsynthesized replies each waste capability or fragment the case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: Address changes always require verify identity → validate new address → update account. Account-takeover reports branch according to device, login, and payment evidence discovered during investigation. Which decomposition is best?

choices.text: Apply dynamic decomposition to both, reasoning that any process can eventually surface evidence worth investigating.
Merge both procedures into one unrestricted prompt and let the model decide, turn by turn, what step to run next without any structure.
Standardize on one fixed pipeline for both, since a single audited sequence is supposedly easier to review than two separate decomposition styles.
Use a fixed verify-validate-update chain for address changes, and adaptive decomposition that branches on device, login, and payment evidence for takeover cases.

questions.explanation: Predictable address changes suit a fixed prerequisite chain, whereas takeover investigations must branch on the device, login, and payment evidence as it's discovered. Applying one decomposition style to both, whether always-dynamic or one merged unrestricted prompt, ignores the difference between known stages and open-ended discovery.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A fraud investigation discovers that the disputed transaction belongs to a second customer profile sharing the same email domain. What should happen to the existing investigation plan?

choices.text: Add a targeted identity-linkage subtask, revise the dependent findings it touches, and leave unaffected work in place.
Finish every subtask from the original plan first, then reopen the case for the new profile only once all of them close.
Restart the investigation from an empty context, discarding evidence already verified, so the new profile gets a fresh review.
